questions.q: Define "imagery" and "metaphor" in your own words, and give one example of each from any Wordsworth poem you have studied.
questions.a: Imagery: language appealing to senses (e.g., "the green earth" — visual). Metaphor: direct equation (e.g., "The child is father of the man" — childhood shapes adulthood). A wrong answer that confuses metaphor with simile ("like a flower") or treats imagery as only visual reveals the student cannot distinguish figurative modes or sensory range.

questions.q: In "The Tables Turned", Wordsworth writes: "One impulse from a vernal wood / May teach you more of man, / Of moral evil and of good, / Than all the sages can." Identify the metaphor here. What is the tenor, what is the vehicle, and what quality is transferred?
questions.a: Metaphor: "vernal wood" as teacher. Tenor = nature/spring woodland; Vehicle = sage/teacher. Transferred quality: authoritative wisdom. A wrong answer that calls "vernal wood" a simile (missing "like/as") or identifies "impulse" as the vehicle shows inability to parse the grammatical structure of the metaphor.

questions.q: Scan the first stanza of "Lines Written in Early Spring" (I heard a thousand blended notes / While in a grove I sate reclined...). List three distinct sensory images, naming the sense each appeals to. Then explain why Wordsworth mixes these senses in the opening.
questions.a: 1. "thousand blended notes" — auditory. 2. "grove" — visual/olfactory. 3. "reclined" — tactile/kinesthetic. Mixing senses creates synaesthetic immersion, mirroring the poem's theme of nature's interconnected harmony. A student who lists only visual images or cannot name the sense has not internalized the full sensory palette.

questions.q: Compare the metaphor of "the world" in "The World is Too Much With Us" ("Getting and spending, we lay waste our powers") with the metaphor of "the child" in "The Child is Father of the Man" (from "My Heart Leaps Up", though not in this chapter, the concept is relevant). How does each metaphor redefine the abstract noun it governs?
questions.a: "The world" = materialistic society (vehicle: a devouring machine) redefines "world" from neutral planet to spiritual predator. "The child" = originator (vehicle: father) redefines "child" from dependent to progenitor of adult identity. A wrong answer that treats both as mere personification misses the redefinition of abstract concepts through metaphorical agency.

questions.q: Critique this student statement: "Wordsworth uses beautiful imagery to describe nature, but his metaphors are simple comparisons that don't require deep analysis." Use evidence from any prescribed poem.
questions.a: The statement is false. In "The World is Too Much With Us", the metaphor "sordid boon" is an oxymoronic compression: "boon" (blessing) qualified by "sordid" (base/ignoble) forces the reader to hold contradictory values simultaneously — industrial progress as both gift and curse. Such metaphors demand analysis of tone, irony, and philosophical tension. A student who agrees reveals a surface-level reading that equates "simple language" with "simple meaning."

questions.q: Write four lines of free verse describing a familiar Indian street scene (a market, a temple courtyard, a monsoon afternoon) using at least three different sensory images and one original metaphor. Do not use "like" or "as".
questions.a: Example: "Turmeric dust hangs in the air — yellow fog / The vendor's call, a brass bell struck / Wet jasmine garlands bruise against my wrist / This lane is a river, flowing without water." (Images: visual, auditory, tactile; Metaphor: lane = river). A poor answer uses only visual imagery, includes similes, or offers a clichéd metaphor ("life is a journey") showing inability to generate fresh sensory-metaphorical fusion.
